content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces a two-level approach to 3D drug-like molecule generation. The approach leverages an equivariant diffusion process to generate a coarse, fragment level structure, which is latter compiled into an actual 3D molecule by aligning selected fragment properties with a library. The model performance is assessed on molecule generation on a quite challenging benchmark dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The approach has certainly the merit of a high effectiveness in the task of 3D drug-like molecule generation. The drug-likeness performance on non-trivial molecules generated starting from GEOM_DRUG is quite impressive. 
The method itself is quite articulated, with several interacting components and different processes operating to incrementally refine intermediate structures before reaching the final generates molecule. On the one hand, all the design choices underlying such components and processes seem reasonable and well-motivated. 

However, the complexity and degree of sophistication of the method makes it very much hard-coded and problem-specific. In particular, the level of novelty when one considers specifically the learning model seems limited. From this perspective the approach seems essentially a quite standard diffusion-based model for graphs, not much different (at the level of the diffusion process) from what EMD (among the others) proposes. The main difference is that such diffusion operates at a coarse level and that the generated fragment embedding is then effectively compiled into valid molecular fragments contextualized to their neighbours in the coarse graph. All in all, this is very nicely engineered for the application, but does not seem to make a strong contribution to the learning methodology. Which instead should be central, given the venue. 

Another concern relates to the empirical analysis: there a single dataset is used, while QM9 is ruled out because of being “too simple”. While I appreciate the quest for realistic and challenging data, I do not see why ruling out the only dataset on which one could have had a wider and more direct comparison with other methods in literature (include EMD which in the original paper is largely assessed on QM9 and only marginally on GEOM_DRUG). This would have also offered the opportunity to test conditional generation under the setting in the Hoogeboom et al 2022 paper. I warmly suggest to add results on QM9 to expand the breadth of the comparison with the related literature and avoid the single-dataset empirical analysis effect. 

Finally, it might be my bad, by I could not find a discussion on uniqueness and diversity of the generated molecules. Statistics about these aspects are needed to rule out the possibility of the model being generating very nice, but very repeated drugs (or very many drugs similar to those in the training data).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Novelty is good if considered as an application paper, but when it comes to the “learning machinery” originality is borderline for this venue. The paper is mostly clearly written and well organized, though the empirical analysis is not fully convincing due to the use of a single dataset.
content.summary_of_the_review: Paper is a borderline one, mostly due how one should be assessing originality and due to some dark spots in the empirical analysis. If novelty aspects as regards the learning methodology can be discussed and stressed further, and extended empirical results are provided, then it can certainly be considered on the positive end of the threshold. In its current form its learning the other way.

Thank you very much for the insightful comments! The response to your concerns are listed below:

**Q1. Clarification on the contribution**

Thanks a lot for pointing it out! And yes, as you mentioned, the assembling part is of fine design towards the specific task which helps us improve the empirical performance. Here we would like to highlight the technical contribution at the learning machinery level. 
The key underlying machine learning challenges of the hierarchical generation framework lie in how to generate structured data under combinatorial constraint, which is shown in Equation 4. Note such a problem has high complexity and brings the so-called "combinatorial exploding" issues. [1] shows even with bigger fragments (motifs) and the autoregressive modeling fashion, the assembling conflict is still very challenging to overcome. And for our non-autoregressive modeling fashion, the complexity further increases exponentially with the structure size. And furthermore, our paper also aims to address a more challenging setting, *i.e.* 3D molecule generation rather than graph generation. In short, our proposed hierarchical diffusion probabilistic model principle solve the combinatorially constrained structure generation problem in an ordering agnostic way, while this perspective hasn't been explored in existing atom-level 3D molecule generation model such as EDM [2]. We believe that the proposed framework could inspire general solutions for other constrained structure generation tasks, such as Dispatching Route Generation [2], Optimal Experiment Design [3], and  Protein Alignment Generation [4]. We will add the above clarifications in the updated paper.
  
**Reference:**

[1]. Jin et al. Hierarchical Generation of Molecular Graphs using Structural Motifs fixed

[2]. Ding et al. XOR-CD: Linearly Convergent Constrained Structure Generation

[3]. Bras et al. From streamlined combinatorial search to efficient constructive procedures

[4]. Ma et al. Mrfalign: protein homology detection through alignment of Markov random fields

[5]. Hoogeboom et al. Equivariant Diffusion for Molecule Generation in 3D

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a fragment-based diffusion model for 3D molecules. Similar to the junction tree VAE approach, the model adopts a two-step generation procedure: it first generates a fragment graph where each fragment is represented by its semantic features (continuous) rather than its actual structure (which is discrete). The 3D coordinate of a fragment is the center (average of the atom coordinates) and generated through a standard diffusion process. In the second step, it learns to predict the fragment types based on their coarse features and assemble the nearby fragments into a full molecule using MPNN.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Representing the fragment as a set of continuous features is an interesting approach and makes it suitable for diffusion based approaches.
2. Node and edge generation follows an iterative refinement procedure (similar to mask language modeling, ordering is learned) instead of an autoregressive process (which requires a specific ordering for an unordered graph).

Weakness:
1. It's helpful to have more comparison with more advanced atom-based methods. If EN-flow and GsphereNet cannot work on larger drug like molecules, why not compare the results on QM9? Though fragment-based methods are probably not that useful for tiny molecules in QM9, at least it serves as a sanity check for the sophisticated method (it's okay if the performance is on par).
2. Many parts of the method are not clearly described in this paper. The exact generation procedure is unclear.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Unfortunately, many parts of the method are not clearly described in this paper.
1. How is the fragment coarse features generated in the first step? Section 4.2 only describes how H_p (position) are generated through a diffusion model. How is H_f (features) generated? 
2. How is the assembly process (second generation step) actually implemented? Section 4.3 only gives a high-level description. A detailed procedure (say an algorithm) would clarify the exact procedure. It's a bit unclear how the three-step tree MPNN is used for generating the fragments and edges.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the proposed hierarchical approach is promising, despite missing comparisons to previous methods and lack of clarity in the method description (section 4). Therefore, I vote for weak acceptance.

content.title: Response to Reviewer gyMh cont.
content.comment:
**Q3. How is H_f (features) generated?**

The original detailed introduction on modeling $H_f$ is in the Appendix. And thanks for the suggestion, we have moved such part to the main text.

Specifically, the modeling process of $H_f$ could mostly follow the diffusion model with Gaussian noise for step $t > 0$. While we find that the $0$-th term for continuous feature $H_f^{\text{int}}$ and $H_f^{\text{cont}}$, i.e. $\mathcal{L}_0$, should be coped with carefully as following to get better empirical performance:

$
    L_0(H_f^{\text{int}},H_f^{\text{cont}})= - \log [\int_{H_f^{\text{int}}-\frac{1}{2}}^{H_f^{\text{int}} + \frac { 1 } { 2 }} \mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{u} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0^{(H_f^{\text{int}})},\sigma_0\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{u}] -  \log\mathcal{N}\left(H_f^{\text{cont}}\mid \frac{\boldsymbol{x}_0^{(H_f^{\text{cont}})}} {\alpha_0}- \frac{\sigma_0} {\alpha_0} \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_0, \frac{\sigma_0^2}{\alpha_0^2}  \mathbf{I}\right)
$

Besides, we take the round function on the $x_0^{H_f^{\text{int}}}$ to get the final sampling results during generation.

**Q2. The exact generation procedure and how is the assembly process (second generation step) actually implemented**


To make it easy to follow, we use **coarse-grained** to refer to the nodes with only the coarse feature aware, and we use **fine-grained** to refer to the nodes whose specific type is already generated. After obtaining the coarse features. At each step of the generation process we conduct the following 3 actions, **(1)** first we predict a focal node among the fine-grained nodes; **(2)** then an edge is chosen to be linked between a coarse-grained node and the focal node; **(3)** the specific fragment type is determined for the new node linked to the graph. The whole generation process is by iterating the above single step. These three predictions are conditioned on the coarse features of all nodes and the fragment type of the fine-grained nodes. Between two generation steps, we conduct iterative refinement to finetune the generated fine-grained nodes. We have revised Section 4.3 and added the generation pipeline in Algorithm **3** in the updated paper.

We extend the experiment part with more results and discussions as shown in the response to Q1. Here we would like to highlight the technical contribution at the learning machinery level. 
The key underlying machine learning challenges of the hierrachical generation framework lie in how to generate structured data under combinatorial constraint, which is shown in Equation 4. Note such a problem has high complexity and brings the so-called "combinatorial exploding" issues. [1] shows even with bigger fragments (motifs) and the autoregressive modeling fashion, the assembling conflict is still very challenging to overcome. And for our non-autoregressive modeling fashion, the complexity further increase exponentially with the structure size. And furthermore, our paper also aims to address a more challenging setting, *i.e.* 3D molecule generation rather than graph generation. In short, our proposed hierarchical diffusion probabilistic model principly solve the combinatorially constrained structure generation problem in an ordering agnostic way, while this perspective hasn't been explored in existing atom-level 3D molecule generation model such as EDM [2].

**Reference:**

[1]. Jin et al. Hierarchical Generation of Molecular Graphs using Structural Motifs fixed

[2]. Hoogeboom et al. Equivariant Diffusion for Molecule Generation in 3D

**Q5. The proposed diffusion model fails to leverage the 3D conformation info during the coarse-grained generation**

Thanks a lot for pointing it out and sorry for making the statements confusing. Compared to the atom-level methods, the coarse-grained generative model seems to not use the whole conformation information of all atoms. Instead, the 3D conformation information of the ground truth is utilized through the form of center coordinates of each fragment in the coarse-grained generation. We would like to emphasize the usage of 3D information in the following two folds: 1).  As shown in Section 4.2, the 3D position-related term $H_p$ is an important component of the objective function of the coarse-grained generative model. And the final position of each fine-grained fragment is actually fully determined in the coarse-grained generation. The conformation quality evaluation in Table.2 shows that the model well learned 3D information. 2). The local structure or conformation is relatively stable, which implies that there are redundant degrees of freedom for using the full atom-level 3D conformation. Given the fragmentized way and connected constraint, we find the center position of fragments could be enough for modeling the 3D information as in the detailed discussion in Section 4.2.

We hope the above response and the updated draft could address your questions!

content.title: Response to Reviewer J3PN cont.
content.comment:
**Q3. Missing comprehensive literature review**

Thanks for pointing it out! To better clarify the difference and contribution of the proposed method, we extend our related work discussion by a comprehensive literature review on hierarchical/multi-scale graph generation works [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] in  Section 2 as suggested. Here we emphasize the key differences between the proposed method and the previous studies in the following three perspectives: 

1. **Semantic guided hierarchies on Graph**: Most previous works derive the hierarchical structure in graph based on some intrinsic rules: Some use the different granularity levels, *e.g.* atom-to-motif [1,2] or edge-to-node [5], as the modeling hierarchy; [3,7] used predefined rules to distinguish different nodes into different levels; [6] utilized the natural topology in graph to get the hierarchy. [4] get the hierarchy by adding latent variables to different module layers of the model. While in our method, we use the learnable decoding module to approximate a semantic guided hierarchy, *i.e.*, a coarse feature could refer to a cluster of property-level/element-level related fragments. Such hierarchies are inspired by the **pharmacophore** to fragment process in traditional drug design.

2. **Non-autoregressive Modeling**: The previous fragment-based molecule generation relies on autoregressive modeling [1,2,5] due to the conflict during the assembling process as shown in Figure 2. The non-autoregressive modeling, though with appealing properties, is mainly limited by the combinatorial exploding during assembling. To the best of our knowledge, we first provide an efficient and effective non-autoregressive solution for fragment-based molecule generation. 

3. **Different Motivations**: In addition to imposing the domain-specific knowledge, the other main reason to involve the hierarchical modeling is to help solve the combinatorial exploding of coping with assembling conflict during generation. We empirically find the proposed framework, by first using a coarse feature to categorize the solution space and then conducting conditional decoding, could significantly reduce the collision in the fragment-based molecule generation setting. We hope the proposed method could also shed light on a more general solution in constrained structure generation. 

**Reference:**

[1]. Jin et al. Hierarchical Generation of Molecular Graphs using Structural Motifs fixed

[2]. Jin et al. Hierarchical Graph-to-Graph Translation for Molecules

[3]. Zhou et al. Misc-GAN: A Multi-scale Generative Model for Graphs

[4]. Kuznetsov et al. MolGrow: A Graph Normalizing Flow for Hierarchical Molecular Generation

[5]. Xianduo et al. Hierarchical recurrent neural networks for graph generation

[6]. Mi et al. HDMapGen: A Hierarchical Graph Generative Model of High Definition Maps 

[7]. Chauhan et al. Multiscale planar graph generation

content.title: Response to Reviewer J3PN cont.
content.comment:
**Q2. The clarification on the error accumulation in auto-regressive approaches**

We agree that our argument for the error accumulation issue needs to be further discussed. Here we elaborate on this problem from both technical and empirical perspectives.
First of all, technically many literature and studies [1,2,3] in other ML fields such as language generation have noticed the error accumulation issues. This means for a step-by-step generation framework, the error in previous steps will make the following generation steps worse and worse, leading to very unrealistic samples.
However, we also noticed this problem is less explored in 3D molecule generation. Our claim actually can be supported by our additional experimental observations. To make it more comprehensive, we conduct the following ablations on autoregressive models with G-Spherenet as the representative:

**Correlation between validity and size for QM9**
| QM9 Size       | 2     | 3     | 4     | 5     | 6     | 7     | 8     |
| -------------- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Valid ( G-Spherenet)     | 0.850 | 0.786 | 0.776 | 0.710 | 0.692 | 0.690 | 0.588 |
| Valid (Ours) | -- | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.950 | 0.953 | 0.991 |

**Correlation between validity and size for $\text{GEOM}_{\text{DRUG}}$**
| $\text{GEOM}_{\text{DRUG}}$ Size | 5     | 7     | 9     | 11    | 13    | 15    | 17    | 19    |
| -------------------------------- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Valid (G-Spherenet)                       | 0.501 | 0.248 | 0.089 | 0.040 | 0.007 | 0.002 | 0.001 | 0.001 |

As shown in the above cases, the performance of G-Spherenet drops sharply with increasing generation steps. This indicates more error is accumulated with longer sampling steps. 

**Reference:**

[1]. He et al. Exposure Bias versus Self-Recovery: Are Distortions Really Incremental for Autoregressive Text Generation?
[2]. Schmidt et al. Generalization in Generation: A closer look at Exposure Bias
[3]. Caccia et al. Language GANs Falling Short

content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a hierarchical model for 3D molecule generation. The model first samples a coarse graph with a diffusion model. In the coarse graph, each node represents a fragment, each edge represents the sharing of an atom/bond between the nodes. Then conditioned on the coarse graph, the model samples the fragment type and the edge connecting the fragments. Additionally, an iterative refinement process is employed to optimize the fragments. Finally, the atom and bond level connection information and positions are post-processed using RDKit from the high-level structures. The model achieved competitive performance on a 3D molecule generation benchmark.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The paper proposed to use a diffusion-based model for hierarchical 3D model generation. The model achieved competitive performance on a 3D molecule generation benchmark.

Weaknesses:
- The paper is poorly written and lacks important technical details in the methodology section.
No white spaces before the left parenthesis.
  - It’s unclear how Q(H|V) in Equation (5) is implemented, and how it is used to train the model.
  - $M$ and $n$ are used without introduction in Equation (6).
  - Section 4.2 did not address the modeling of $H_f$.
  - The second paragraph of Section 4.3.1 is difficult to understand. It’s unclear what “determined fragments” and “determined nodes” refer to. Training details of the GNNs of focal, edge, and node were not mentioned in the paper. It’s unclear how to provide supervision for these neural nets.
  - The paper did not mention how to obtain the fragments and how to unambiguously fragmentize the molecules in the dataset for training.
  - Important details such as iterative refinement should be put in the main text instead of the Appendix sections.
  - Section 4.3.2 lacks clarity. Does subgraph selection refer to the determination of the 2D graph structure? And fragment alignment for 3D structure? What does the RDKit and Kabsch algorithm do?
  - The first and second rows of Figure 4 are not consistent, and this inconsistency causes confusion. There should be 2 nodes in the MPNN illustration in the second row instead of 5 nodes.
  - It seems that the arrow directions in the Three-Step Tree MPNN in Figure 4 are reversed.
  - It’s unclear how to use a fixed-dimensional diffusion model to generate molecules of different sizes.
- The conformation quality evaluation in Section 5.2 is debatable. Not sure whether it’s fair to use the conformations generated by RDKit as oracles for comparison because the proposed method used RDKit to generate 3D graphs in Section 4.3.2.

content.comment:
## Concerns on the experiments

**Q9. Towards the conformation quality evaluation in Section 5.2**

This is indeed a great point! Firstly, we would like to clarify that RDKit is only used to generate the local conformations of subgraphs and hence the whole conformations are mainly determined by the positions of the coarse set feature during assembling. Actually, it's pretty common to take advantage of the RDKit to generate local structures [1], which is fast and accurate.
Besides, we also realized that using RDKit to evaluate the conformation also brings in a train-test discrepancy. The conformation of molecules in $\text{GEOM}_{\text{DRUG}}$ is generated by an approximate Molecule Dynamics process using the software XTB and CREST [2]. And our model is trained on such conformation distribution instead of RDKit-generated distribution. 
To provide a fair and reasonable evaluation, we conduct exactly the same process on the generated molecules to get the oracle conformations for comparison and the new results are provided in the following:

|             | COV-atom $\uparrow$ | MAT-atom $\downarrow$  | COV-frag $\uparrow$ | MAT-frag $\downarrow$  |
| :---        |    :----:   |    :----:   |     :----:   |        ---: |
|    EDM     |     0.489    |   1.349   |  0.097   | 3.234   |
|    $\text{CS-Diff}_{\text{E}}$  | **0.546** |  **1.121**   | 0.153    |  2.583   |
| $\text{CS-Diff}_{\text{P}}$   |    0.490     | 1.166    | **0.202** | **2.431** |
| $\text{GEOM}_{\text{DRUG}}$   | 0.589    | 0.494   | 0.435    | 1.494   |

And with the Molecule Dynamics simulated ground truth, our methods have shown a consistent improvement in conformation quality compared to the EDM baseline. We will update the conformation evaluation part as suggested in the revised paper. 

**Reference:**

[1]. Jing, Bowen, Gabriele Corso, Jeffrey Chang, Regina Barzilay, and Tommi Jaakkola. "Torsional Diffusion for Molecular Conformer Generation." NeurIPS (2022).

[2]. Axelrod et al. GEOM, Energy-annotated Molecular Conformations for Property Prediction and Molecular Generation

We hope the above response and the updated draft could address your questions!

content.title: Response to Reviewer uVJs cont.
content.comment:
**Q5. Data fragmentization and implementation details**

We added the detailed fragmentization and implementation details in the revised paper.
In short, we first get simple rings within molecular graphs according to RDkit and then break the molecules into chemical bonds and simple rings. The rings sharing more than two atoms will be merged together. And the intersecting atom of more than three fragments is extracted from the graph and added to the final fragmentized structure. Similar approaches have been widely applied in many other related works [1,2,3,4].

**Reference:**

[1]. Jin et al. Junction Tree Variational Autoencoder for Molecular Graph Generation

[2]. Jin et al. Hierarchical Generation of Molecular Graphs Using Structural Motifs

[3]. Maziarka et al. Mol-CycleGAN: a Generative Model for Molecular Optimization

[4]. Chen et al. A Deep Generative Model for Molecule Optimization via One Fragment Modification


**Q6. Section 4.3.2 lacks clarity. Does subgraph selection refer to the determination of the 2D graph structure? And fragment alignment for 3D structure? What does the RDKit and Kabsch algorithm do?.**

Yes, as you mentioned,  subgraph selection refers to the determination of attachment between fragments for the 2D graph structure. And fragment alignment is used to plug the predicted local conformation into the global coordinate systems to get the atom 3D structure conformation. We have reorganized and rewrote the original Section 4.3.2 into the last paragraph of Section 4.3 and Section 4.4 in the revised paper as suggested to make the presentation clearer. And we discuss the usage of RDkit and Kabsch algorithm in the following:

- RDkit is used in both the 2D graph determination and atom 3D conformation generation. For 2D attachment determination, we need RDkit to get local structures for different attachments. And we selected according to the RMSD compared to previously generated fragment centers. In atom 3D conformation generation, RDkit is used to get the substructure conformations, and then such conformations are assembled according to calculated rotation matrixes and translation vectors by the Kabsch algorithm. 

- Kabsch algorithm is used to get the rotation and translation factor to transform local structures into the global coordinate system. Given the RDkit generation local structures, the Kabsch algorithm solves the optimal rotation and translation to align the fragment center of RDkit generated structure and our generated fragment center.  

We have revised the description to make it clearer and provided a pseudocode in the appendix. 
 


**Q7. The inconsistency and arrow directions in Figure 4.**

Thanks for pointing out the inconsistency and reversed arrow directions. Here we have rerendered Figure 4 to make the MPNN illustration consistent.

 
 **Q8.how to generate molecules of different sizes with diffusion model**

Molecules of different sizes are padded to the max size with the help of corresponding mask vectors. During generation, we first sample the size of the molecule, i.e. the number of fragments in our setting. The distribution of size is counted from the dataset. 
And then construct the mask according to the sampled size to initiate the exact number of atomic coordinates and types.  Then the diffusion model could process and generate molecules of different sizes. We added detailed discussions in the revised paper.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful and detailed suggestions! We address the concerns in the following:

## Concerns about the writing

Thanks again for the detailed comments which definitely help us to improve the paper. We have carefully followed your suggestions and revised all mentioned parts in the updated version.  

**Q1. How the Q(H|V) is implemented and how it is used in training**.

- Here $Q(H|V)$ refers to the process of obtaining the coarse set features ($H = [H_f, H_p]$) given the fragment ($V$). The coarse set features have two components, $H_p$, and $H_f$. 
As we showed in section 4.2, $H_{f}$ could be obtained according to either property-based or element-based mechanisms. And the position-related variable, $H_p$, is defined as the center coordinate of the fragment $V$ which could be calculated by averaging the coordinates of all atoms. 
- During training, the above process is firstly applied to the training data to get the $H$ for both the *coarse set diffusion* objective and the *fragment assembling* objective according to Equation (5). 

We have added the above discussions in Section 4.1 of the revised paper. 

**Q2.  M and n are used without introduction in Equation (6).**

Sorry for the missing introduction of notations. $M$ here stands for the number of fragments in the molecule and $n$ corresponds to the dimension of coordinates which is 3 in our experiment settings. We have added the introduction right after Equation (6) in the updated version. 

**Q3. Lack of the introduction on modeling $H_f$ in Section 4.2.**

The original detailed introduction on modeling $H_f$ is in the Appendix. And thanks for the suggestion, we have moved such part to the main text.

Specifically, the modeling process of $H_f$ could mostly follow the diffusion model with Gaussian noise for step $t > 0$. While we find that the $0$-th term for continuous feature $H_f^{\text{int}}$ and $H_f^{\text{cont}}$, i.e. $L_0$, should be coped with carefully as following to get better empirical performance:

$L_0 (H_f^{\text{int}},H_f^{\text{cont}})= - \log [\int_{H_f^{\text{int}}-\frac{1}{2}}^{H_f^{\text{int}} + \frac { 1 } { 2 }} \mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{u} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0^{(H_f^{\text{int}})},\sigma_0\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{u}] - \log\mathcal{N}\left(H_f^{\text{cont}}\mid \frac{\boldsymbol{x}_0^{(H_f^{\text{cont}})}} {\alpha_0}- \frac{\sigma_0} {\alpha_0} \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_0, \frac{\sigma_0^2}{\alpha_0^2}  \mathbf{I}\right)$

**Q4. The presentation of the second paragraph in Section 4.3.1, training details and supervision signal**



Following your suggestion, we rewrote the whole section 4.3 of the revised paper. Here we further explain the mentioned confusing parts:

- “determined fragments” and “determined nodes” refer to the nodes whose fine-grained fragment types have been already generated, *i.e.* predicted by the node network in previous steps. 

- training details and supervision signal: During training, we start by first randomly sampling a connected subgraph. Then a random leaf node is picked, and we simulate the generation of this node: We keep all the fine-grained fragment types and edges of the subgraph except the selected node. And for all nodes not in the subgraph, we only maintain the coarse features.  $\phi_{{\text{focal}}}$ is trained based on the above feature to predict the parent of the selected node among the nodes in the subgraph; $\phi_{\text{edge}} $ are trained to predict the edge link between the parent node and the selected node among all other coarse-grained nodes. Note here we use the coarse feature of the selected node; And $\phi_{\text{node}}$ learns the fine-grained fragment type of the selected node. For the iterative refinement part, we just randomly mask a node's fine-grained feature on randomly sampled subgraphs, and $\phi_{\text{refine}} $ is trained to reconstruct its masked fragment type. Detailed implementation and objectives can be found in the Appendix. 

The above discussion has been added to the revised paper.
